speaker: Derek Lowe
title: Derek Lowe, PhD: A Medicinal Chemist’s Thoughts on Drug Discovery and the Future of Pharma
question: In pharmaceutical development, what operational factors beyond regulatory paperwork make clinical trials so expensive to run?
guest: It's a labor-intensive process, and it starts just with patient enrollment—tracking down the right patients that fit the profile you're looking for, making sure they have the disease as you understand it, and that they don't have other conditions that are going to warp your data. So patient selection and enrollment is tedious and expensive. Then running a properly statistically valid, double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trial requires more patients than you would figure because you need a robust placebo group and often several arms for different dosages and dosing schedules. You also have to coordinate logistically across multiple hospitals and medical centers, making sure everyone runs it the exact same way and handles blinded data properly, because mishandling blinded data will blow you up immediately. Specialists and companies that help run trials charge a lot of money to do this. Then there's the time involved—weeks, months, even years for slow diseases like Alzheimer's—taking hundreds or thousands of precisely timed physician visits, wellness checks, and blood draws that must happen the exact same way every time. You get up into hundreds of thousands of dollars per clinical trial subject.

points.core: Screening patients to match strict disease criteria without confounding comorbidities is costly.
points.note: Accept: expensive recruitment, narrow inclusion/exclusion criteria, or filtering out patients whose other conditions skew results. Do not credit: generic mentions of finding patients without explaining screening complexity.

points.core: Randomized placebo groups across multiple dosing arms multiply required trial sample sizes.
points.note: Accept: statistical power requirements for control/placebo arms, dose-ranging cohorts, or multi-arm schedules expanding enrollment. Do not credit: vague statements that trials need a lot of people.

points.core: Coordinating standardized blinded protocols across multiple medical centers requires expensive specialist vendors.
points.note: Accept: multi-site logistics, CRO fees, site monitoring, or maintaining strict blinding integrity across hospitals. Do not credit: blaming FDA administrative overhead or paperwork.

points.core: Long disease timelines require thousands of repeated, strictly standardized clinical patient assessments.
points.note: Accept: multi-month or multi-year follow-up requiring scheduled physician visits, lab draws, or uniform longitudinal readouts. Do not credit: generic remarks that drug development takes a long time.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Most of the cost comes from people, patients, and time rather than paperwork.

Patient recruitment and retention is typically the biggest driver: finding eligible participants is slow, many sites enroll few or no patients, and dropouts force over-enrollment. Each delay extends the trial, and every extra month carries fixed costs for staff, sites, and vendors.

Site operations are also costly. Sponsors pay investigators and coordinators, cover per-patient procedure fees (scans, labs, biopsies), and fund start-up at dozens or hundreds of sites across multiple countries. Monitoring adds heavily to this, since on-site visits to verify source data against trial records have traditionally consumed a large share of budgets.

Protocol complexity compounds everything: more endpoints, procedures, and visits per patient raise per-patient costs, and mid-trial amendments trigger retraining, re-consent, and system changes.

Other major items include manufacturing and distributing the study drug (plus comparators and placebos, often with cold-chain logistics), data management and statistics, central laboratories and imaging review, safety monitoring, and contract research organization fees.

Finally, large sample sizes and long follow-up, especially in late-phase trials for chronic diseases, multiply all of these costs.

models.label: Gemini Carbon

Beyond regulatory compliance, clinical trial costs are driven primarily by site operations, patient logistics, clinical procedures, and specialized supply chains. Recruiting, screening, and retaining eligible patients—especially for narrow or rare indications—requires extensive outreach and high-volume screening, while slow enrollment and patient dropouts extend timelines and compound daily overhead. Sponsors must pay substantial fees to hospitals, principal investigators, and research staff at dozens or hundreds of sites, alongside Contract Research Organizations whose clinical monitors verify site execution and source data.

The medical care itself is resource-intensive, encompassing frequent blood work, genetic or biomarker profiling, biopsies, and advanced imaging such as MRIs or PET scans, often shipped to centralized laboratories to ensure standardized measurement. Meanwhile, manufacturing small-batch investigational drugs, purchasing expensive commercial comparator therapies for control arms, packaging blinded doses, and running global temperature-controlled cold-chain logistics require dedicated infrastructure. Finally, operating randomization and electronic data systems, funding independent safety monitoring boards, running biostatistical analyses, and reworking operations during mid-trial protocol amendments add substantial ongoing expense.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Most of the cost comes from running studies with large numbers of patients over long periods across many sites. **Recruitment and retention** are usually the biggest problem. Most trials miss their enrollment timelines, and every month of delay adds site fees, staff and vendor costs. Sponsors pay for advertising, screening patients who turn out ineligible, and travel support to keep participants enrolled. **Per-patient site costs** are also high. Investigators bill for every visit, scan, biopsy and lab test the protocol requires, and in oncology this can come to tens of thousands of dollars per patient.

**Protocol complexity** multiplies those costs: more endpoints and procedures mean more work at each visit. Mid-study amendments are common, and Tufts research puts each one at hundreds of thousands of dollars. **Monitoring and data management** add more, especially on-site source-data verification by contract research organization (CRO) monitors. **Clinical supply** needs specialized manufacturing, placebo or comparator drugs, blinding, cold-chain shipping across countries, and wasted overage. Finally, **high failure rates** mean the money spent on unsuccessful trials has to be recovered through the ones that succeed.

Beyond regulatory paperwork, clinical trials are expensive largely because recruiting and retaining eligible patients is slow and difficult. Narrow eligibility criteria and competition for participants often force sponsors to open dozens or hundreds of clinical sites across multiple countries, each requiring contract negotiations, staff training, and ongoing operational management. High screening failure and dropout rates further lengthen timelines, and every extra month adds substantial fixed costs for clinical research organizations, site coordinators, and investigator fees.

Protocol complexity also drives expenses sharply upward. Modern trials frequently require specialized diagnostic imaging, central laboratory testing, biomarker assays, and comparator drugs purchased at commercial prices, alongside clinical-grade manufacturing, blinding, and temperature-controlled global supply chains. On top of direct medical costs, sponsors pay heavily for continuous quality control, including on-site and remote monitoring, source-data verification, and specialized data-management systems to ensure trial integrity. Finally, mid-trial protocol amendments—often triggered by recruitment bottlenecks or emerging safety data—cascade into re-training, re-consenting, and system updates that compound overall budgets.

Clinical trials are expensive because sponsors have to recruit eligible patients and keep them in the study long enough to measure outcomes. Sites spend staff time screening people who may never enroll, and slow recruitment can force sponsors to open more sites or keep them running longer. Each site needs trained clinicians and coordinators to conduct visits, administer treatment, collect samples, and track side effects.

Sponsors also pay for tests, imaging, and central labs, as well as manufacturing, packaging, and shipping the study drug and any placebo or comparator. Across sites, teams monitor how the trial is run, resolve discrepancies in the data, and analyze the results. Large trials multiply these costs across patients and sites, while long follow-up keeps staff and systems working for months or years.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra

Clinical trials are expensive because they have to find the right patients, deliver treatment consistently across sites, and follow participants long enough to measure outcomes. Recruitment can be especially costly when a condition is rare or eligibility criteria are narrow. Screening takes staff time and often requires tests, even for people who never enroll.

Each site needs trained investigators, research nurses, coordinators, and pharmacy staff. Repeated visits, lab tests, imaging, and procedures add costs for every participant. Running a blinded trial may also require manufacturing a matching placebo and packaging, storing, and shipping supplies so neither patients nor clinicians can tell which treatment was assigned.

Teams must also monitor safety, check data across sites, and resolve missing or inconsistent results. When the outcome of interest is uncommon or takes years to appear, a trial may need thousands of participants and years of follow-up. Slow enrollment extends the time that sites, staff, and systems must stay in place.
